526.title: Strong and trustworthy
526.hook: the best to hire is the strong and the trustworthy (28:26)
526.carry: the kind of job nobody will check
526.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 28:26 when speaking of hiring, leadership and work ethic, holding that a person given a role should be both capable and trustworthy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: haya', modesty you can see in a walk. Your line was modesty is a walk.

Every hiring manager has a list: experience, references, a good interview. Musa has none of it. He's a fugitive with no money, no letters, no home, sitting in a stranger's house in Madyan. He has told the old man his whole story, and the old man has said, don't be afraid, you've escaped from the wrongdoing people. Then one of the daughters speaks up and gives him a reference. Two words, and she has seen him earn both.

Hire him, she tells her father. Pickthall: "the best (man) that thou canst hire is the strong, the trustworthy." In Arabic, al-qawiyy al-amin. Qawiyy is strong, able to do the work. Amin is trustworthy, from the same root as amana, a trust, and iman, faith. She has seen both. Strength at the well, where he watered a whole flock that had been waiting behind the shepherds. Trustworthiness on the way home: commentators tell, from a report attributed to 'Umar, that Musa asked her to walk behind him and call out the way, so he wouldn't be looking at her as she walked. That detail is from commentary, not the verse. Either way, she'd watched him work, and watched him behave when no one else was looking. Both words matter. Strength without trust is a danger: a capable person you can't rely on. Trust without strength is a disappointment: a good person who can't do the job. The same pair turns up once more, in Surah An-Naml, from an unlikely mouth: a jinn offering to fetch the Queen of Sheba's throne says he is strong and trustworthy for the job. The old man takes his daughter's advice. He offers Musa marriage to one of his daughters, for eight years of work, or ten if he chooses. Musa answers: whichever term I complete, let there be no injustice to me. A contract between two people who each had reason to trust the other. A hadith in Bukhari warns that when trust is lost, the Hour is near.

segments.voice: Think of the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid: a job, a class, a household, caring for someone. Ask honestly where you're strong but not quite trustworthy, a corner cut, a promise let slide, and where you're trustworthy but not yet strong. If you pray, you can ask for strength and trust together.
Al-amin. The daughter's word for Musa: trustworthy, safe to trust with the work. Today's word.
Your line: the kind of job nobody will check. Trust shows when no one is watching. See you tomorrow, then.

527.title: Qarun's keys
527.hook: the rich man told not to exult, but to do good as Allah did good to him (28:76–77)
527.carry: do good as good was done
527.howItsDone: Muslims read Qarun's story as a warning against pride in wealth, and often quote 28:77, do good as God has done good to you, when speaking about charity and balance in worldly life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-amin, trustworthy, one of the daughter's two words. Your line was the kind of job nobody will check.
screen: `THE KIND OF JOB NOBODY WILL CHECK.`

segments.voice: Not the gold. The keys. Al-Qasas tells of Qarun, from Musa's own people, whose treasures were so many that the keys alone, the verse says, would have been a heavy load for a band of strong men. The story never says how much gold there was. It measures the wealth by the weight of its keys. And his own people, the verse says, gave him advice.

The advice comes in five parts, holding this world and the next together. Don't exult; God doesn't love the exultant. Seek the home of the hereafter with what God has given you. Don't forget your share of this world. Then, Pickthall: "be thou kind even as Allah hath been kind to thee". In Arabic, ahsin kama ahsana Allahu ilayk: do good as God has done good to you. The word is ihsan, excellence, doing beautifully. Nobody tells him to give it all away. Enjoy your share; just let the good flow on in the direction it came. And fifth: don't spread corruption on the earth. Qarun's answer turns the story. I was given this only because of knowledge I have. I earned it. He doesn't deny God exists; he leaves God out of the account. Then he goes out before his people in all his finery. Some sigh: if only we had what Qarun has. But those given knowledge say, woe to you, God's reward is better for whoever believes and does good. Then, the verse says, God caused the earth to swallow him and his house, and no crowd could help him. The next morning, the ones who envied him are saying: so God gives freely to whom He wills, and holds back. Classical commentators identify Qarun with Korah, whose rebellion in the Book of Numbers also ends with the ground opening. The keys were never the problem. The problem was believing they were self-made.

Then choose one of them, or a little money, that could go on to someone who needs it, and picture who. If you pray, you can thank God for what came to you before it goes on.

528.title: Left alone to say "we believe"?
528.hook: do people think they will be left to say we believe and not be tested (29:2)
528.howItsDone: Muslims understand trials, hardships and even blessings as tests from God, and many recite 29:2–3 and ask God for steadfastness in times of difficulty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Qarun and his keys, wealth he thought was self-made. Your line was do good as good was done. Today, a new surah.

A goldsmith has a lump of metal that looks like gold. Right color, heavy, and the customer swears it's pure. But she doesn't take anyone's word for it. Into the crucible it goes, and up goes the heat. Whatever isn't gold separates and burns away, and what's left is what it really was all along. Surah Al-'Ankabut, the Spider, the twenty-ninth, opens with a question a lot like that crucible.

After the opening letters, alif, lam, mim, the surah asks. Pickthall: "Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction?" The next verse answers: those before them were tested too, so that God would make known those who are truthful and those who lie. The word for being tested comes from the root of fitnah, today's word. In the old Arabic dictionaries, the root's first meaning is the goldsmith's: putting gold or silver into fire to separate pure from impure. From there it spread: a trial, a temptation that pulls at you, and elsewhere turmoil and civil strife, when a whole community goes through the fire. The Qur'an even calls wealth and children a fitnah. So the test isn't only the hard thing; it can be the good thing, and what you do with it. Tradition places this surah in Mecca, when early Muslims were being pressured, some tortured, for their faith. The verse doesn't promise them comfort. It tells them this is what faith is like: saying we believe is the first step, and the fire shows what it's made of. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the people most severely tested are the prophets, then those most like them, and that a person is tested according to the strength of their faith. Read that way, a test is not a punishment and not a sign of being forgotten. In the Qur'an's picture, the crucible is a way of being taken seriously.
screen: `LEFT TO SAY WE BELIEVE?` · `FITNAH: GOLD IN THE FIRE.` · `TRIAL, TEMPTATION, TURMOIL.` · `TESTED AS FAITH IS STRONG.`

segments.voice: Run through the day ahead, or the day behind, and find one place where something pushed on what you say you believe: impatience, a corner to cut, gossip to join, a good thing that could make you proud. Don't judge it; just see it clearly, as a goldsmith looks at what comes out of the fire, and name it: that was the test. If you pray, you can ask to be steady through it.
Fitnah. A trial: from a root meaning to put gold in the fire, then any test, temptation or turmoil that shows what faith is made of. Today's word.

529.title: The spider's house
529.hook: the frailest of houses is the spider's (29:41)
529.howItsDone: Muslims read the parable of the spider's house as a reminder to rely on God rather than on idols, wealth or status, and the surah is named Al-'Ankabut for this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fitnah, gold in the fire, the trial that shows what faith is made of. Your line was faith is tested.

Early morning, after a damp night, they're everywhere: webs strung between fence posts, across window corners, between stems in the garden, each one beaded with dew, catching the light. They're beautiful, and a spider worked hard on each one. Then you walk through one without seeing it, and it's gone, a few strands on your sleeve. Surah Al-'Ankabut is named for that web, and for one verse that uses it as a picture.

The verse is a parable. Pickthall: "The likeness of those who choose other patrons than Allah is as the likeness of the spider when she taketh unto herself a house, and lo! the frailest of all houses is the spider's house, if they but knew." Three things to notice. First, patrons: awliya', protectors, the ones you lean on. The verse is about where people put their weight. Second, the spider isn't lazy or foolish. She builds, and what she builds is intricate and real. As shelter, it just can't hold: it keeps out nothing, not rain, not wind, not a careless hand. Third, the ending: if they but knew. As if the people leaning on the wrong thing could see it, if they looked. Before this verse, the surah tells of peoples, Nuh's, Ibrahim's, Lut's, 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh, who trusted in their strength, their wealth, their idols, and found it was thread. There's also a story often told from the Prophet's journey to Medina: when he and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr, a spider spun a web across the entrance, and the pursuers passed by. That's a story people tell, and its chains are weak; the Qur'an mentions the cave but not the spider. So the same creature appears in two pictures. In the verse, the web is the frailest of houses. In the story, a frail web, held by God, protects. What matters, in both, is who you lean on.
screen: `OTHER PATRONS: WHAT YOU LEAN ON.` · `SHE BUILDS, AND IT CAN'T HOLD.` · `IF THEY BUT KNEW.` · `THE WEB AT THE CAVE: A STORY TOLD.`

segments.voice: Think about what you reach for when things wobble: your phone, someone's approval, a bank balance, being busy, being right. None of these is bad in itself, any more than the spider's silk is, but pick one and ask honestly: if the wind came, would this hold me, and what would? If you pray, you can lean your weight, for this minute, on God.

530.title: Defeated, then victorious
530.hook: the Romans have been defeated, and within a few years will win (30:2–4)
530.howItsDone: Muslims read the opening of Surah Ar-Rum as a prophecy fulfilled in the Byzantine recovery under Heraclius, and as a reminder that the outcome of events belongs to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-'ankabut, the spider whose house can't hold. Your line was not the spider's house. Today, a new surah.

News of a far-off war reaches Mecca. Two empires are fighting: the Romans of Constantinople, whom historians now call the Byzantines, and the Persians. The Romans are losing. In Mecca, far from the fighting, people take sides. A report in Tirmidhi says the Muslims wanted the Romans to win, since they were people of a scripture, and the Quraysh wanted the Persians, who, like them, had no scripture. Then a surah opens with a headline.

Surah Ar-Rum, the Romans, the thirtieth. Pickthall: "The Romans have been defeated". In the nearer land, the verses go on, and after their defeat they will be victorious, within a few years. The phrase is bid' sinin. Bid' means a handful, a small number; the same report in Tirmidhi gives it as between three and nine. And on that day the believers will rejoice in God's help. The Quraysh laughed. The report says Abu Bakr was so sure that he made a wager with some of them, before wagers like that were forbidden, and when the Romans won, he won it. Tradition says the emperor Heraclius turned the war. Some commentators link the believers' rejoicing to the same season as their own victory at Badr; others read it differently, and scholars have discussed exactly which events fit. But the verses don't stay with empires. The next lines say: God's is the command, before and after. Then the surah widens into a long meditation on signs: night and day, rain on dead earth, the cycle of life. In the surah's picture, a defeat isn't the end of a story. It's a chapter. The defeated can win within a handful of years, and the One who turns it is the One who brings green out of dead ground.
screen: `THE ROMANS HAVE BEEN DEFEATED.` · `BID' SININ: A HANDFUL OF YEARS.` · `ABU BAKR'S WAGER.` · `GOD'S IS THE COMMAND, BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you're losing right now: your health, a project that keeps failing, a relationship gone cold, a habit that keeps winning. Don't pretend it isn't a defeat; hold it, then imagine the same scene a handful of years from now, turned around, and notice what small step points that way. If you pray, you can ask for help with it.

531.title: Love and mercy between you
531.hook: He made mates for you to find rest in, and put love and mercy between you (30:21)
531.howItsDone: 30:21 is widely recited at Muslim weddings and written on wedding cards and gifts, and Muslims often describe marriage through its words: rest, love and mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Romans, defeated, then victorious within a handful of years. Your line was within a few years.

At many Muslim weddings, at some point, someone reads one particular verse. You'll often find it on the invitation too, in Arabic calligraphy, sometimes in gold. Plenty of people know it without knowing much else of Surah Ar-Rum. It's short, and it sits in a list of God's signs, between the creation of human beings from dust and the creation of the heavens and earth. It puts a marriage, an ordinary household, right there among them.

Pickthall: "And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." In that, the verse ends, are signs for people who reflect. From yourselves: of the same kind, the same nature. Then the purpose: li-taskunu ilayha, that you might find rest in them. The root s-k-n means stillness, settling, dwelling; it gives sakina, tranquility, and maskan, a home. So a spouse is somewhere you come to rest, the way you come home. Then two words, carefully chosen. Mawadda: warm affection, love you can see. And rahma: mercy, from the same root as the womb, and as ar-Rahman. Commentators have enjoyed setting the two side by side. Some say mawadda is the love of the early years, and rahma what carries a couple when looks fade and someone gets ill. Others say mawadda is love you feel, and rahma is care you choose, even on days the feeling is thin. Either way, the verse doesn't stop at love; it adds mercy, as if love alone won't always be enough. And God put them there, ja'ala baynakum: not you made them, He placed them between you. Many Muslims hear that as a reason for gratitude, and as a standard. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the best of you are those who are best to their families. The Qur'an counts a quiet kitchen, two people at rest with each other, as a sign as real as the sky.
screen: `HELPMEETS FROM YOURSELVES.` · `SAKAN: A PLACE TO COME TO REST.` · `MAWADDA, AND THEN RAHMA.` · `HE PUT THEM BETWEEN YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of the person you come home to, or would most like to: a spouse, a parent, a sibling, a friend, a child, and picture their face at the end of an ordinary day. Ask where your love for them is easy right now, and where it needs mercy instead. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.
Mawadda. Warm, visible love, one of the two things, with rahma, mercy, that Ar-Rum says God placed between spouses, so they could find rest in one another. Today's word.

532.title: Tongues and colors
532.hook: the diversity of your languages and colors is among His signs (30:22)
532.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 30:22, 49:13 and the Prophet's farewell sermon to teach that no language, people or color is above another, and that only taqwa distinguishes people before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mawadda and rahma, love and mercy placed between two people. Your line was love and mercy between.

Stand in the courtyard of the Great Mosque in Mecca at any hour, and listen. Indonesian, Urdu, Turkish, Hausa, Bosnian, Malay, Bengali, Somali, French, English, Arabic in a dozen accents. Faces of every shade, from every continent, walking the same circle, many in the same white cloth. Some pilgrims come home talking less about the buildings than about the crowd. The verse right after yesterday's has a word for what they saw.

Pickthall: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge." Look at the company the verse keeps. The heavens, the earth, and in the same breath, the fact that people speak differently and look different. Human variety sits on the same shelf as the sky. Not a problem to solve, and not a ranking: a sign, an aya, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an. Who is meant to read this sign? Men of knowledge, in Pickthall's English; in Arabic, al-'alimin, those who know. As if the more you learn about people, the more there is to see. Surah Al-Hujurat says something close: We made you nations and tribes so that you might know one another, and the noblest of you with God is the most mindful of Him. And in his farewell pilgrimage sermon, reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by taqwa. His first community already looked like that: Bilal from Abyssinia, Salman from Persia, Suhayb, called the Roman. This week ran from Al-Qasas through Al-'Ankabut to Ar-Rum: al-amin, do good as good was done, faith is tested, al-'ankabut, within a few years, love and mercy between. And today, the widest: difference is a sign.
screen: `LANGUAGES AND COLORS BESIDE THE SKY.` · `A SIGN FOR THOSE WHO KNOW.` · `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · `NO ARAB OVER NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY TAQWA.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you see often whose first language isn't yours: a neighbor, a colleague, the person at the corner shop, a classmate's parent. Wonder for a moment what they speak at home, and how they'd say hello or thank you in it. If you pray, you can thank God for one person whose difference has taught you something.
Aya. A sign, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an: what Ar-Rum calls the variety of human languages and colors, beside the heavens and the earth. Today's word.
Your line: difference is a sign. Variety is something to read, not to rank. That's the week.

chat.says: Does the Qur'an see different languages and skin colors as a problem?
options: No. Ar-Rum lists them among God's signs, beside the heavens and the earth.
It doesn't mention them; it only speaks of believers and unbelievers.
It sees them as differences to be erased in one shared culture.
chat.meaning: 30:22 puts the difference of your languages and colors among God's signs, with the heavens and the earth, for those who know.

aya.meaning: a sign; also a verse of the Qur'an
